subject: Agriculture
title: Pesticides and the Green Revolution
description: A short lesson to help you apply Pesticides and the Green Revolution.

hook.text: Dense monocultures of high-yield crops are pest magnets. The Green Revolution needed chemical protection.

buildup.text: Pesticide use in India increased 200-fold between 1960 and 2000, paralleling Green Revolution adoption.

discovery.text: Chemicals controlled insects, fungi, and weeds that thrived in the new uniform, fertilized fields.

twist.text: Pests evolved resistance. Farmers applied more chemicals, creating a treadmill of escalating inputs.

climax.text: Health effects on farm workers—poisoning, cancer risks—became a growing but underreported crisis.

punchline.text: The revolution packed a punch—but the chemicals punched back.

quiz.question: How much did pesticide use increase in India during the Green Revolution era?

details.summary: The Green Revolution's high-yield monocultures required significantly more pesticide input than traditional diverse farming systems. This topic covers how pesticide use escalated alongside yield increases, the health and environmental consequences, and the push toward integrated pest management.
details.whyItMatters: Pesticide use in developing countries increased tenfold during the Green Revolution. The resulting health impacts on farmers, environmental damage, and pest resistance are among the most serious negative legacies of agricultural intensification.
takeaways: Green Revolution monocultures were more vulnerable to pest outbreaks than diverse systems
Pesticide use in developing countries increased roughly tenfold from 1960 to 1990
The brown planthopper crisis in Asian rice showed how pesticides can worsen pest problems

faq.question: Why did the Green Revolution increase pesticide reliance?
faq.answer: High-yield monocultures planted over vast areas create ideal conditions for pest outbreaks—large, dense populations of genetically similar plants. This replaced the natural pest regulation of diverse traditional farming.

faq.question: What was the brown planthopper crisis in Asian rice?
faq.answer: In the 1970s, insecticide spraying on Green Revolution rice in Indonesia and the Philippines killed the natural predators of brown planthopper. Without predators, planthoppers multiplied exponentially, destroying more rice than before spraying began.
